newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW - Baer technician sees U.S./Europe splits.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Baer technician sees U.S./Europe splits.

text.p: Reinhard Stutz, technical analyst for securities markets at Bank Julius Baer, sees signs of a divergence in recent U.S. and European stock market trends.
Stutz said in an interview that in the past, such market behaviour would have been highly unusual if not unthinkable.
"Older traders say when prices break lower in New York, we in Switzerland break as much, if not worse. But most recently this was not the case. We have decoupled a bit," he said.
He also said technicals may be a good indicator of market psychology, which was a valuable quality in the current U.S. market following its protracted advance.

Stutz said he does not provide prognoses, but instead works to find divergences which are used to determine the timing to profit from trends. He also looks at fundamentals, which lie outside the realm of pure technical analysis.
He said one reason for possible divergences may be due to the fact that European economies are lagging a couple of years behind the U.S. recovery.
He also cautioned that currencies, as opposed to interest rates, could play a decisive role for European stocks near-term.
Stutz said a decoupling versus the U.S. was evident in German and French, as well as for U.K. stocks, although to a lesser degree. The trend was also seen in Swiss stocks.
Based on weekly charts for the U.S. Standard & Poor's 500, and the blue-chip Swiss Market Index, he said that when U.S. markets had staged a correction recently, Swiss markets moved largely sideways.

"The correction in Switzerland during the Wall Street correction was not so massive. Prices in Switzerland tended more sideways. We nearly had a sell signal in Swiss stocks -- but nothing happened," he said.
The subsequent recovery in the U.S. market also has not been as buoyant as in Switzerland, he noted.
With respect to divergences, in terms of recent performance, U.S. and Swiss stocks based on weekly closing prices, were still in an upwards trend.
But Stutz said charts showed prices rising while the relative strength index, at least in the U.S., appeared to be in a trend showing lower highs since late in 1996.
"That is the problem we have in America. We have new highs with lower RSIs," he said. If the weekly RSI appears to be peaking, it would be a good argument for going short, he said.
He added the S&P currently had a first upper target of 855 and a second target of 880. The S&P ended Tuesday at 837.66. The RSI is now roughly at 70.
With respect to the Swiss market, he saw a maximum upside target for the SMI currently of 5,400. The SMI closed at 5,042 on Monday.
Baer follows around 90 stock indices, as well as 400 of the 500 S&Ps, and the German FAZ shares.
With respect to Swiss stocks, Stutz made the following observations based on technicals:
-- Swissair had been recommended at 1,050 Swiss francs, and it briefly took out 1,350 francs. If the test of that level is successful there could be further advances.
-- Oerlikon-Buehrle was right at a key level of 150 Swiss francs, with further gains possible to 170 to 180 francs if that level is overcome.
-- Union Bank of Switzerland, unlike the other two big Swiss banks, had not yet returned to its old high of roughly 1,500 francs. Swiss financials still appeared intact.
-- Sulzer broke out at 980 francs and appeared to have further technical potential for gains.
-- Novartis was still in an upwards trend.
